lines.text: What if the Earth started to spin faster, a little more every second, and nothing in the universe could stop it? You are standing on the equator, and you are going to watch what happens, minute by minute, until the planet can't take it anymore.

lines.text: Here are the rules. The Earth keeps its size, its shape, its air and its water. Only the spin changes, and it only ever gets faster. On screen there is one number that matters: the length of a day. It starts at twenty-four hours, and by the end it will have fallen to about an hour and twenty-four minutes. Under it is the second number: how fast the ground is moving under your feet. Nothing resets, and nothing slows. The planet is not a perfect ball, and we will skip a great deal of real physics, so treat every number as a first guess.

lines.text: Right now, one day lasts twenty-four hours. Or almost: the Earth turns once in twenty-three hours, fifty-six minutes. Standing on the equator, the ground carries you around at about sixteen hundred and seventy kilometers an hour. You never feel it, because everything moves with you. What you do feel is a tiny push outward. You weigh about a third of a percent less than you would on a planet that did not spin.

You weigh one point four percent less than on a still Earth, four times what you feel today. A seventy kilogram person feels like about sixty-nine.

Winds like that would strip the surface, and they would only be the beginning.

lines.text: And then the oceans begin to move. A spinning planet pushes water outward, toward the equator, exactly as it pushes you. Today the Earth already bulges about twenty-one kilometers wider at the equator than from pole to pole, and the ground has had billions of years to settle into that shape. Speed the spin up quickly and the ground cannot adjust in time. At a twelve hour day, the water wants to stand about thirty-three kilometers higher at the equator than at the poles, extra, compared with today. The whole ocean is only about three point seven kilometers deep. So the water does not simply rise. It drains toward a belt around the equator, while the poles dry out. This is a rough, first guess, but the direction is certain: land near the poles emerges, and your own coast is flooded.

lines.text: The sky has another problem. Storms are steered by the planet's spin, through the Coriolis effect, and that steering grows in step with the spin rate. At a six hour day it is four times stronger than today. At the edge of floating, it is seventeen times stronger. Weather systems would be squeezed into tight, fast bands, and the calm of an ordinary afternoon would be gone. Nobody could forecast it, because nobody has seen a planet like this.

lines.text: Meanwhile, the calendar breaks. The year does not change, because the Earth still goes round the Sun once. But every day gets shorter, so a year contains more days. Right now, at a six hour day, a year already holds about fourteen hundred and sixty days. By the end, it would hold over six thousand, with a sunrise every eighty-four minutes, and you would be asked to sleep eight times a day.

lines.text: Not everyone on Earth would feel the same thing. At the poles, the ground only turns on the spot. Nobody there is carried around at all, and they would weigh the same as ever. At forty-five degrees north, you move at seventy percent of the equator's speed, and the push outward is only half as strong. The farther you stand from the equator, the longer you keep your weight. But the water leaves the poles first, so the stillest place on Earth would stand high and dry.

At that speed, the push outward exactly cancels gravity. You weigh nothing. You are no longer standing on the Earth. You are orbiting it, one stride above the surface, with the whole equator going by beneath you.

lines.text: And past that point, the equator can no longer keep its own rock. This is as far as a simple sum can honestly take us. A real planet is not a perfect ball, and what happens next depends on how strong the Earth is. But the direction is clear: the spin would tear the equator apart. First the loose things would go, then the sea, then the rock.

lines.text: Of course, nothing in the real universe could ever do this. To spin the Earth that fast you would have to put in about six times ten to the thirty-first joules, nearly three hundred times the spin energy it has today. That is every drop of sunlight the Earth receives, for about eleven million years.

lines.text: So the next time you stand still, remember the speed you are carrying. You are already moving at sixteen hundred kilometers an hour. You only have to go about seventeen times faster to leave the ground behind. The day would have to shrink from twenty-four hours to an hour and twenty-four minutes. That is the whole distance between standing and flying, and it is why a planet's spin can never be a small thing. Thanks for watching.
